subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF MAILBOXES FROM TORONTO STREETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Toronto residents, particularly the elderly and those in poor health, are experiencing hardship and inconvenience as a result of Canada Post's decision to remove some of the 1,800 red mailboxes located throughout Metropolitan Toronto.
In the worst cases, mailboxes located just outside or just across the street from senior citizens' highrise apartments have been removed, forcing people to walk blocks further in hazardous winter conditions to mail their letters. If we add to this the distinct possibility of higher postal rates in the near future it is clear that the Canada Post strategy of reduced service at higher cost leaves no room for fair and balanced treatment of the taxpayers who have to use the postal system. I urge the Government to rethink its strategy and replace the mail deposit boxes which have been removed from their locations in Toronto.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF HELSINKI EMBASSY-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with deep regret that I have to rise in this House to raise the issue of the recently leaked closure of the Canadian Embassy in Helsinki, Finland. I appreciate and applaud the Government's objective in applying restraint to come to terms with the legacy of past government deficits. However, on behalf of the Canadian Nordic Parliamentary Friendship Association I implore the Government to reconsider its decision regarding the presence of a Canadian Embassy in Helsinki, Finland. There are several well-known historical facts in support of this request, not to mention recent significant Finnish investment in our country, along with advanced technology in ice-breaking, which strengthen the need for this important post.
The saving of $2 million per year is very small consolation when, at the same time, the National Capital Commission announces a plan to spend $15 million to replace the conventional asphalt pavement in front of our Parliament Buildings with some sort of red ceremonial pavement.

subsubtopic: U.S.S.R.-ANDREI SAKHAROV-RETURN TO MOSCOW FROM INTERNAL EXILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my New Democratic Party colleagues I want to say how pleased we were this morning to learn that Soviet authorities have allowed Andrei Sakharov, the Nobel Peace Prize winner and outspoken defender of human rights, to return home to Moscow from internal exile in Gorky. Andrei Sakharov has been a beacon to those around the world who believe that no matter how difficult and dangerous it may be, the freedom to speak out freely without threat of punishment is a basic human right that no state authorities can take away.
This was a welcome gesture by Mr. Gorbachev and his colleagues in the Kremlin. Let us hope that it signals a growing acceptance in the Soviet Union of the dignity of the individual. Among the civilized community of nations there is no place for those who imprison their people solely for the crime of speaking out for what they truly believe.
At this time of year, when we celebrate the birth of one whose life was dedicated to peace and harmony among all men and women, it is time to reflect on how we see each other as citizens of planet earth. We must learn to live together and cooperate for the betterment of all peoples and future generations. Mr. Speaker, the Soviet Union took one small humanitarian step forward today. Let us hope that it is just the beginning.

Mr. Speaker, this week a delegation of prominent members of the U.S.S.R.

December 19, 1986
Supreme Soviet visited Ottawa. At a meeting with Canadian Senators and parliamentarians a spirited two-hour discussion ensued. In answer to my queries, Mr. Afanasiev, Chief Editor of the Soviet newspaper Pravda, denied the existence of the Soviet-conducted Ukrainian famine of 1933 which caused the death of some six million Ukrainians. He also replied that the Baltic States of Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania invited the Soviets to incorporate them with the Soviet Union, but said nothing of the hundreds of thousands shipped to Siberia.
Despite the differing Canadian opinion on these matters, dialogue between our countries must be promoted. A member of the Soviet delegation declared that an exchange of our parliamentarians would be most valuable. Mr. Speaker, Canadians agree. I look forward to my visit as well to foster dialogue, greater understanding and peace between the Soviets and Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALMOST TOTALLY ENGLISH PRESS CONFERENCE HELD IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is altogether unacceptable that a Government which poses as the defender of the French language in Quebec would send one of its Ministers, a francophone no less, to hold a press conference in Montreal almost exclusively in English. Mr. Speaker, this occurred only a few days after his leader and his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), stood up in that same city to reaffirm their conviction with respect to the supremacy of French in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, according to the information I got from the journalist who wrote about this, the Minister of State (Youth) (Mr. Charest) spoke half the time in French and half the time in English the day before yesterday in Montreal when he unveiled what was practically a carbon copy of a Liberal program for young people which was launched in August 1984. The people with him could not speak French. This kind of procedure made the newspaperman wonder whether Montreal had suddenly been proclaimed an English city.
The Minister was probably so ill at ease that he did not want to announce in French the money involved because it is very little compared with what young people need. This is probably why no Member of the Official Opposition had been invited to the press conference, neither in French, nor in English.

Last Tuesday, Mr. Speaker, I was in Quebec City to meet with more than 400 early retirees who had been denied unemployment insurance benefits by this Government. I was there with my friend, the Liberal Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), but I was quite surprised to realize there was no Conservative representative, not even a Member from the Quebec City area nor from Levis.
The executive of the association, ARSAC, wrote an open letter to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). In this letter they say that the Conservative policy in the field of unemployment insurance is unacceptable, arbitrary, unfair and discriminatory against the unemployed in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I agree with these 400 people, I agree with ARSAC, and I ask that the Government reconsider its policy before Christmas. Mr. Speaker, why not offer a Christmas gift?

speechtext:

subsubtopic: JOBS IN JEOPARDY AT GENERAL MOTORS PLANT IN SAINTE-THERESE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, the U.S. free trade negotiator, Mr. Peter Murphy, took the liberty of sticking his nose into Canada's affairs by warning the Canadian Government against awarding an interest-free loan to General Motors in Sainte-Therese, which would help save 4,000 jobs.
"If Quebec and Ottawa decide to take action", he warned, as quoted in La Presse, "-we'll have to take a very close look at this".
Mr. Speaker, since when did the Americans start minding our business? Ever since the Canadian Government started showing signs of weakening and the Americans received a clear message that they could do what they felt like doing. For instance, that they could go through the Canadian North with their submarine Polar Sea and impose tariffs on softwood lumber. The image projected by the Canadian Government has led the Americans to try and dictate the kind of policies they feel the Canadian Government should adopt.
This morning at a press conference, the Prime Minister merely said: "The Canadian Government will make the decisions on Canadian affairs." That is merely saying the obvious. We urge the Prime Minister to be more forthright and say quite frankly that he is going to help save jobs at General Motors by subsidizing the enterprise, together with Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin) tabled in the House his document on new directions for the financial sector. The message it contains will help the Canadian economy adjust to new communications technology and management techniques. The Government will allow the integration of financial services.
More good news: insurance agents or brokers will continue to occupy the field of retail insurance.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has managed to adjust to technological change while maintaining every consideration for the very personal relationship that exists, in our neighbourhoods, municipalities and cities, between the insurance agent and his client.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the Government has recognized the dedication and competence of our local insurance agents.
Canadians will continue to have their own insurance agents, thanks to the Conservative Party.

[DOT] (mo)

Mr. Speaker, for many years Canadians have looked for a clear policy on the regulation of financial institutions. With the announcement of new directions for the financial sector by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), we have now received a decisive and clear message.
Our nation's independent insurance agents were very concerned that the integrating of financial services might have resulted in banks and trust companies selling property and casualty insurance, something that would have sounded the death knell for small independent insurance brokers.
Many of us, as Members of Parliament, have been working closely with our insurance agents to let the Minister know of our concerns. In the Minister's announcement we heard a sensible ownership policy, a strong framework for smarter regulation, improved supervision, and, most important, a clear unequivocal statement that banks, trust companies and other financial institutions will not be allowed to sell insurance at the retail level.
This is a victory for insurance agents and a sign that the Minister of State for Finance and the Government have listened and acted wisely.

subsubtopic: NORTHERN BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF TAX MORATORIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last February the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) declared his intention to tax northern benefits. One problem faced by many northern residents is that the Government, after nine months, has been unable to determine the value of subsidized housing.
The general guideline of fair market value is unworkable in many communities where there is little or no private sector housing. The Department of Public Works has now indicated that some Canadians will be asked to pay income tax on up to an extra $1,700 a month, money they never saw and never had. Where actual salaries are low or moderate, this will obviously create instant poverty.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PAST SUCCESSES AND FUTURE WISHES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we leave this place for the Christmas break, it is a good time to review the highlights of the past year and the prospects for the year ahead. There were some great days for British Columbia in 1986, among them, of course, the outstanding success of Expo 86, which gave British Columbia a chance to show its stuff to the rest of the world. We hope that many of the millions who visited Vancouver and Expo will return to British Columbia and explore the fascination and beauty of the province.
We are also very proud of British Columbian Rick Hansen whose courageous voyage around the world has stirred our hearts and raised our understanding of the needs and potential of Canadians who suffer from physical handicaps.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF WAR ON POVERTY SOUGHT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Christmas is a time to be with family, a time to give and share, and a time to be grateful. It is also a time to contemplate the plight of the poor and disadvantaged in Canada.
This Christmas over a million Canadian children are being raised in families with incomes below the poverty line. There are 3.6 million of our fellow Canadians living below the poverty line. Poverty is a human tragedy and a national disgrace. All Canadians, regardless of where they live and what they do, are entitled by right to a decent standard of living. Our major priorty in 1987, as parliamentarians, must be to declare war on poverty.
Our goal as parliamentarians must be to ensure that all Canadians live above the poverty line. As we leave Parliament for Christmas, let us not forget the loneliness and despair of the poor and disadvantaged. Let us come back in January and work together with the new resolve to end poverty. Let us come back in 1987 and work toward providing decent housing, educational opportunities, and meaningful employment for those who have not shared in the economic benefit our country is capable of providing for each and every Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake tabled in the House the report of the Government Operations Committee concerning Canada Post's five year corporate plan. On behalf of all members of the House, 1 would like to thank the committee members for their diligent work.
As requested under provisional Standing Order 99(2), Mr. Speaker, the Government will be tabling in a few moments a formal response to the report presented by the Standing Committee. I would like to take this opportunity to address the most important issues raised by the committee.
Mr. Speaker, as Members will recall, my colleague, the Minister of Finance announced last spring that Canada Post would be required to eliminate its operating deficit by fiscal year 1988-89. Our objective was for Canada Post to improve service and reliability while managing both its finances and its operations more efficiently and effectively. Our resolve in this remains undiminished.

In response to the orientation set by the Government, the senior management and Board of Directors of Canada Post prepared a five-year corporate plan in which the corporation detailed the measures it proposed to take in order to improve both service and over-all efficiency.
When the details of the plans were scrutinized by the parliamentary Committee on Government Operations, it became apparent that some of the measures that the Corporation proposed were of concern. In particular, the committee devoted much of its time and attention to the impact of proposed changes in postal service on rural Canadians.
The committee has indeed done tremendous work. The Government has had an opportunity to examine the report of the committee and is in general agreement with its observations and recommendations.
In recognition of the changing demographics of rural Canada, Canada Post has been eliminating rural lot line delivery routes for years. The corporate plan proposed measures that would have further removed lot line service for some 100,000 rural Canadians. In response to concerns raised by the committee, the corporation has advised me that it will
Statements by Ministers
not proceed at this time on the replacement of rural lot line services.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation
speechtext:
This change will be reflected in Canada Post's next corporate plan.
On the subject of the possible amalgamation of some rural Post Offices, I am in agreement, as is the corporation, with the point made by the committee that a simple amalgamation formula cannot be imposed arbitrarily and uniformly on a country as broad and diverse as Canada.
Canada Post recognizes the need to be sensitive to local concerns that vary from community to community. During the hearings, the President of Canada Post made the commitment that there will be no amalgamation without local consultations and that in the future a 90-day notice will be given of proposed service changes to permit this process to take place.
While amalgamations of rural Post Offices must take place, it will be done on an opportunity basis, wherever possible, due to retirement of a postmaster or some such other vacancies. Where this is not possible, a human resource management plan will be developed.

I was pleased to note that the commitee is in general agreement with the proposal of Canada Post Management to involve the private sector on a broader scale through franchising in the provision of counter services in rural and other areas. The small businesses and entrepreneurs of Canada can do an excellent job in meeting many essential consumer needs in this country through franchising. As Members already know, 25 per cent of Canada Post's retail outlets are already managed by the private sector.
The subject of second class mail privileges for newspapers, periodicals and books is part of the larger issue of cultural subsidies for which my colleague the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) is responsible.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind Hon. Members that the Government is presently paying more than 70 per cent of the cost of sending publications through the mail. This particular approach has not been revisited since 1969 and, accordingly, the Department of Communications with the assistance of Treasury Board and Canada Post will be consulting with the publishing industry on this issue over the next several months. In the interim Canada Post will be proceedings with modest increases to the rates of published materials effective July 1st, 1987.
Of most concern to the committee were proposed postal rate increases for weekly newspapers. The Government shares the concern expressed by the committee on the impact these increases could have had on weekly newspapers. I have received assurances from Canada Post that there will be no increase in the rates for weekly newspapers.

With respect to services in urban areas, the committee also heard testimony regarding the faulty installation and a particular design problem associated with supermailboxes.
In response to these problems, members of the committee expressed concern with the security of mail delivered by this means. Canada Post has given its assurance, both to the committee and to the Government, that these problems will be eliminated prior to the installation of any new supermailboxes. With regard to disciplinary and legal action resulting therefrom, I understand Canada Post is giving these matters full consideration.
Canada Post is also taking steps to meet another concern voiced by the committee, the need to ensure that the services available to the public through supermailboxes are accessible to physically handicapped customers.

In many areas of the country, particularly in small towns, Canadians have never had door to door postal delivery services. In fact, Mr. Speaker, only 54 per cent of Canadians currently receive door to door service.
As members of this House know, the cluster box concept, as an alternative to door to door delivery was developed by Canada Post under the previous Government. Then as now, it was apparent that the cost of extending door to door delivery to new areas of the country was prohibitive. Supermailbox services, properly installed, are a vast improvement over the old green community mailbox delivery mode introduced by the previous administration or for that matter, general delivery, and represent an efficient means of servicing new growth areas at a cost considerably less than the $500 millions associated with the extension of door to door service in all new subdivisions.

Finally, the committee carefully considered the planned two cent increase in the basic letter rate and concluded that the increase is not excessive. The Government concurs with this conclusion. Therefore, gazetting of the rate increases will take place at the earliest opportunity. Further increases to the basic letter rate which will henceforth become effective on January 1 of each year, as necessary, will be held to not more than the rate of inflation.
I want to be very clear today that the Government is maintaining the approval it gave last October of the CPC corporate plan for the period 1986-87 to 1990-91. We are holding the CPC to its projected loss of $30 million in 1987-88 and profits of $53 million, $44 million and $58 million in the following three years, and its full commitment to an improved postal service for Canadians.
Considerable progress has already been achieved by Canada Post Corporation. For example, over the last two years, the volume of mail processed has increased while at the same time using 2,000 less employees. Absenteeism has been reduced by 26 per cent. Expenses other than salaries in 1985-86 were close to 2 per cent lower than the previous year.
The committee expressed the view that while improvement has taken place since the corporation was established, further progress was called for.
[ Translation]
For example, first class mail's reliability has improved by an unprecedented 4 per cent since the summer.
Both the CPC Board of directors and management recognize that the financial discipline imposed by our fiscal framework is an essential element in their efforts to move the mail with service reliability, economy and efficiency.
They know that financial viability is the best guarantee of security that any corporation can give to its employees, and to its customers. They are heartened to receive this confirmation of their operating plan because it is a clear manifestation of the confidence and support which the Government has placed and continues to place in them over the difficult months and years ahead.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the members of the committee, and the others who praticipated in the hearings, for their work. I believe that their report, and the results stemming from it, are a clear indication of the success of this Government's intentions to incorporate the views and talents of all private Members into achieving workable solutions to the important issues of the day.

As I said earlier, now is the time to let the corporation get on with the job.

The Minister said in his remarks that Canada Post "detailed the measures it proposed to take in order to improve both service and over-all efficiency". Member of the Opposition was in accord with the Government-the report on which the Minister has made his statements today is a complete whitewash. Does it mean that the Member of Parliament will be notified or will he or she only receive notice in his constituency mail after a decision has already been
Statements by Ministers
taken? It is important for us to know just exactly how that consultation process will take place.
In terms of closing down post offices on the so-called opportunity basis, that is wrong. That criteria should never be used, and I will tell the Minister why. I have a postmistress in my riding who is in her sixties. She has been saying for some time that she wishes to quit her job and retire. However, the citizenry have been telling her not to quit because if she does they will lose their post office. What kind of pressure is that to be placing on people? Mr. Speaker, with all the talk about privatizing post offices,

Mr. Speaker, I wish to come right to the point. From the report of the committee and from the Minister's response it has been clearly demonstrated that the majority of the committee members were nothing more than yes-men. They were yes-men to the Minister and yes-men to the President of Canada Post. I say yes-men deliberately. Perhaps if there had been some female Members of Parliament on the committee there would have been some more humanity expressed by the majority, as opposed to the callous attitude that was taken with regard to postal service.
The Minister's statement today only deals in a token way with postal service. In effect what the Minister has done is dealt with the tip of the iceberg. When a sailor is out on the ocean he has to know not only what is taking place above the water-line but what is taking place below. He has to know not only where is the tip of the iceberg but where the bulk of it is beneath the water-line. That is what led to the sinking of the Titanic. Sitting across from me is the captain of the Titanic. His ship is going down. Postal service is going down and all the Minister deals with is the tip of the iceberg, that little part above the water-line.
I wish to give some credit where credit is due. What is being done that is positive has to do with lot line service in rural areas and with weekly newspapers. The Minister deserves some credit. He has put a halt to the reduction in lot line services in rural areas, according to the words in his statement. I hope he lives up to those words. He has also put a halt to the increase in rates for weekly newspapers. So the Minister and the committee deserve some credit in this regard.
However, the people who deserve the most credit are members of the Canadian public. I say that because it is they who spoke out. It is they who let the Government know in no uncertain terms that they are fed up with further reductions in postal service. It is because of the strong public outcry that the Government has backed down and buckled under with respect to these two issues.
To place the matter in perspective, this is just the tip of the iceberg. These are but two token elements of the over-all postal plan. What we have to examine is what lies below the waterline, what is left undone. We must examine where the real problems that will sink the postal service lie, the problems which will cause untold damage to Canadians in terms of their postal service.
What is below the water-line is rural service and rural post offices. The way the Minister deals with these matters is by saying that there is a need for a sensitivity to local concerns. That is no assurance that rural post offices will not be closed. In fact, the Minister has said that amalgamations will go ahead. Thus in the future we will see closures of rural post offices. What will be required is for people to continue to speak out, and to speak out loudly in order that their post offices not be closed.
The Minister said in his statement that there would be no amalgamations without local consultation and that in the future a 90-day notice will be required. It is already a requirement under existing legislation and existing post office policy that notice be given. That requirement has not been respected. It has not been effective. What faith can we have in the Minister with respect to him changing his ways regarding to rural post offices?
Having regard to rural post offices, I wish to deal directly with the Minister's claim about franchising, about turning over all of the rural post offices to the private sector. Let me point out that the Minister intends to do the same thing with urban post offices. What we are talking about is turning over all of the post offices in the country to the private sector in the name of efficiency and convenience. If we need more convenience and efficiency in the post office, that could be done equally as well in the public sector as in the private sector.
The danger in what is being done is not only that there will be a reduction in service but, when these contracts are let, there will be a real temptation for abuse. There will be

December 19, 1986

temptation for the Government to use these contracts as another patronage tool.
Over the last few days we heard about the way Citizenship Court judge positions are used as patronage tools. Here the Government is opening up a whole new line of patronage gifts to pass out. The difficulty with that is that the Government can abuse that process at the cost of service.
Another item that is below the surface of this postal plan is the issue of the superboxes. In his statement, the Minister talked about dealing with technical problems and he assured us that there will be no new superboxes put in place until all technical problems are dealt with. Why were the technical problems not dealt with in the first place? Why should we have any more confidence in his assurances today than we have had in his assurances in the past? On a number of occasions the Minister assured us that superboxes were an improvement in service, that they had been fixed and that they would work. Each time that was not the case. Experience proved otherwise.
What people need and want is equity in service. I give the Minister credit for putting a stop to the introduction of superboxes in place of lot-line service in rural areas. If the Minister can do this for rural citizens, why can he not do the same thing for those who live in urban areas? Why does he not say that there will be no second-class citizens, just as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said, not only in rural areas but in the cities as well? I challenge the Minister to live up to that principle and to apply the policy on an equitable basis.
I would like to deal briefly with the rates charged for mailing books, periodicals and religious magazines. I will sum up as quickly as I can, Mr. Speaker. There are a few important points that I must make.
While the Minister deserves credit for saying no to an increase in weekly rates, he has failed to mention in his statement, either inadvertently or through poor writing, the issue of religious publications. The survival of publications of religious and voluntary organizations continues to be threatened by this policy. As well, national magazines such as Maclean's and Saturday Night, instruments of communication that help keep this country together, are also threatened by the policy with which the Government is going ahead.
The Government is promising consultation and I hope that consultation will be significant rather than token, as it has been up until now. Unfortunately, the statement made by the Minister is not surprising. It contains some specific token elements on which the Government has capitulated in the face of public opinion. However, the over-all impact of this statement is that the Government is going full steam ahead with cutting back on postal service and with raising postal rates. Not only will rates be increased by two cents this year but they will be increased annually.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
I am informed
Order Paper Questions
by the Departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and National Health and Welfare as follows:
1.	The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare issued an Information Letter to all interested parties, such as consumer groups, industry, associations, other governmental departments, etc., in July, 1983, proposing new regulations pertaining to the control of food irradiation. In effect, these regulations would remove food irradiation from the food additive provisions in Division 16 of the Food and Drug Regulations and establish a new division in the regulations specific to this physical process. The proposed new regulations contain definitions, detailed pre-clearance requirements and inspection procedures appropriate to food irradiation. In addition, under the new regulations, irradiated foods meeting the pre-clearance requirements and deemed acceptable from a human health standpoint would be listed individually in a table to this new division together with any restrictions on irradiation sources and dose limitations. Only those foods listed in this table would be permitted to be irradiated (within the limitations described) and sold in Canada. It should be noted that no relinquishing of control of food irradiation from a public health point of view will occur if these proposed regulations are adopted. In fact, these regulations will allow more effective regulatory control of this process than currently exists.
2.	(a) The pre-clearance requirements proposed would require testing to determine the minimum dose needed to be efficacious in individual applications. In addition, data which would indicate the effects, if any, on the nutritional quality of the food and data establishing that the irradiated food has not been significantly altered in chemical or physical characteristics to render it unacceptable for human consumption would also be required. Furthermore, tests to establish the safety of irradiated foods would be required in those instances where toxicological testing on a world-wide basis to date has been deemed to be inadequate.
(b) In so far as labelling is concerned, this issue falls under the purview of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It should be noted however, that consideration of food irradiation as a process does not preclude labelling. See also part 5 on this matter.
3.	(a) (i) (ii) As a means of informing the public and other interested parties, the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare issued and Information Letter on these new regulatory proposals in July, 1983. In addition, officials have given numerous speeches and media interviews on this subject and the Department of National Health and Welfare will continue to disseminate information on health and safety related issues as well as regulatory aspects of food irradiation. The Health Protection Branch expects to issue by February, 1987, a second Information Letter addressing the issues and concerns raised in response to the proposed regulatory changes and delineating the Branch's final position.
(b) Not applicable

December 19, 1986
Order for Return
4.	The Health Protection Branch distributed to various groups, organizations, individuals, et cetera approximately 7,000 copies of the Information Letter delineating the new regulatory proposals. To date, only 17 detailled responses have been received. Of these responses, 7 were from food companies, 2 from trade associations, 2 from provincial governments and 1 each from a scientific association, consumer association, contract irradiator, food irradiation equipment supplier, foreign embassy and public advocacy organization. The majority of the responses favoured food irradiation and the regulatory position proposed by the Department. In addition, however, the Health Protection Branch has received hundreds of letters from private individuals who, for the most part, oppose food irradiation for a variety of reasons including philosophical opposition to irradiation and nuclear related processes in general, health and safety concerns as well as relating to possible lack of adequate labelling.
5.	Yes. In July, 1983, the Bureau of Consumers Affairs of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs issued Trade Communique No. 39 requesting comments from food manufacturers and trade and consumer associations on a number of possible options to be considered for the labelling of irradiated foods. A second Trade Communique, No. 50, was issued in November, 1985, which summarized to responses to the options provided in Trade Communique No. 39 and offered for comment a proposed labelling scheme for irradiated foods. A draft regulation was recently discussed informally with a selected segment of the food industry and the Consumers' Association of Canada.
(a)	No final decision has yet been taken. The design and content of the final CCAC labelling regulation will be to ensure that consumers will be able to make informed choices and purchasing decisions between irradiated and non-irradiat-ed food products.
(b)	Not applicable.
6.	The Department of National Health and Welfare has not conducted any specific toxicity tests on irradiated food. Nevertheless, over the years several hundred toxicity studies including lifetime feeding studies in laboratory animals have been carried out world-wide on a large number of irradiated foods. Staff scientists as well as international experts have reviewed and evaluated in detail the results of these studies. Based on these data it has been concluded that the consumption of foods irradiated at practical dose levels (up to 10 kiloGray) would not pose a health hazard to consumers. Departmental scientists will continue to maintain close scrunity over the safety of this process as well as any proposed new applications and the need for further safety testing will be reassessed should any relevant new studies become available.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to be able to introduce Bill C-17 for third reading. This Bill will eliminate the petroleum and gas revenue tax, effective October 1, 1986. You will know, Sir, that this was a very speedy and quite a substantive response to the deteriorating position in the oil and gas sector in western Canada in particular. It is a demonstration of the concern that the Government has shown to the plight of that industry and the effects it is having and has had on the economies of western Canada, particularly in the smaller communities so greatly affected by the slow-down in the oil and gas service industry.
Members will recall that the PGRT was originally announced in October, 1980 as part of the National Energy Program, and first came into effect in 1981. It was a very controversial Bill at the time and much despised in western Canada. The Progressive Conservative Party in opposition took a very strong position against the impact of this tax, the impact of the tax on drilling activity and therefore on the jobs of those people reliant on the oil and gas service industry. We fought the Bill strongly at that time and we made a commitment in the 1984 election campaign to remove the tax. This is the culmination and the fulfilment of that commitment.
Major changes were made to the PGRT and the Western Accord signed with the producing provinces in March, 1985. The most important change was the introduction of a rate phase-out schedule which terminated the PGRT at the end of
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
1988, and the elimination of the PGRT effective March 31, 1985 for all new wells and new enhanced oil recovery projects.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the economic environment facing the oil and gas industry today is much different than it was in early 1985. The oil industry should no longer be subject, in our judgment, to a discriminatory tax on its drastically reduced revenues that have occurred since the Western Accord was signed. The Government's original intention was to phase out the PGRT over a three-year period. We felt that was a fair approach, taking into account the very tough fiscal conditions under which the federal Government was required to operate. We felt that that was an appropriate schedule after having reviewed the matter with the industry and with the provincial Governments concerned.
The Bill before us today proposes to eliminate the tax completely, effective October 1, 1986. It also proposes to increase the annual small producer credit from $500,000 to $2 million, effective May 1, 1986; to exempt from PGRT all revenues attributable to synthetic oil production, effective May 1, 1986, and to provide retroactive relief to January 1, 1986 for individuals and corporations. For corporations this relief will allow up to $1.5 million to be included in the income eligible for the small producer credit. For individuals, this deduction replaces the existing $10,000 deduction. This is a very helpful initiative on the part of the Government to take account of the difference in the impact of the phase-out that had been previously announced as it affected small producers and producers supported by royalty holders.
The Bill will also introduce other changes to terminate the PGRT Act, including a sunset provision for the use of the accumulative offset account against income taxes. Most of these changes were announced to taxpayers on September 17, 1986. I believe this is a very worth-while initiative, an initiative that recognizes the changed situation in western Canada as it relates to the oil and gas industry. I urge the House to give expeditious consideration to this legislation and hopefully deal with it completely today. I want to thank members of the legislative committee for their expeditious review of the Bill and to thank both opposition Parties for the support they have given in moving this legislation along.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to say a few words on this legislation. As I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) make his statement I recalled the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announce that as a result of the Western Accord we could expect to see the creation of 300,000 new jobs. I was wondering what millennium she was referring to. Obviously it had nothing to do with reality. The conditions in the oil patch, particularly in Alberta, are now bordering on the catastrophic. People are waiting to see what bold initiative the Government will take to bring some life back to the oil patch, particularly given the importance of self-sufficiency in this critical resource. We are not talking about potatoes or codfish or coal, we are talking about a resource which is critical to the western way of life.
The resource sector is on its knees and requires extraordinary initiatives by the Government. Yet the best it can do is to have the Minister of Finance make some comments at third reading stage of the PGRT Bill. As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) indicated, the Government has done virtually nothing. He referred to the NEB report tabled this past week. That report points out that hundreds of millions of dollars have been returned to the multinational oil companies. It indicates that rather than investing those funds back in Canada they are going to the corporate headquarters in the U.S. That does not come as a particular surprise to many of us. We predicted that that would happen if there was no requirement to invest these massive funds in the oil patch here. No, the Government said it was going on the basis of the good faith of the oil companies. It knew they would behave as good corporate citizens and reinvest all this money in the western economy. They are not doing that.
If you were to look carefully at the press release from the Independent Petroleum Association on September 8, you will see that the chairman, John Howard, said:
My discussions with our member companies indicate that the bulk of the money saved by the elimination of the PGRT will be reinvested in the industry.

I do not think it is unrealistic to expect all of the PGRT money to be reinvested. After all, that money was derived from Canadian resources and ought to be reinvested in Canada. Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
The NEB report also pointed out a very serious problem facing Canada. It indicated that we ought to become extremely concerned because self-sufficiency in the very critical cultural resources of oil and natural gas is now in jeopardy. That self-sufficiency is a long way off because they predicted that in the next few years, because of the lack of exploration, the lack of activity in the oil fields and potential oil fields of Canada, we will again become a major importer of foreign oil. That is a very sad comment considering the tremendous reserves which exist within our borders.
I would like to indicate very clearly the position which New Democrats have taken on the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax. When the PGRT was first introduced by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Allan MacEachen, of the previous Liberal administration, in November, 1980, we opposed the Bill. The legislation was introduced for first reading in the House of Commons on January 26, 1981 as part of a much larger Bill, C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. The Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act proposed an 8 per cent tax on gross revenue from the production of oil and gas.
During debate on Bill C-57 in 1981 the New Democratic Party opposed the PGRT for four broad reasons. The first reason was that the PGRT was in fact a royalty on a natural resource rather than a tax on corporate income and, therefore, was constitutionally dubious. We also opposed it because it was a regressive tax which would affect producers differently, depending on their size, with smaller producers being hit harder by this drain on their revenues than the larger multinational integrated producers.
In our speeches on second reading of Bill C-57 we predicted that the PGRT would hurt federalism and aggravate already acrimonious relations with the western provinces. As we all know only too well in this House, the divisions between western Canada and the rest of Canada were deep as a result of the PGRT. We predicted that when the Bill was first introduced in 1980.
Finally, we said at that time that we believed that more taxes on petroleum and gas would mean more lost jobs and less activity in that industry. It has become very clear since the PGRT was introduced that it was a major factor in the resultant decrease of economic activity in the oil patch.
I have just finished reading the speech made by our then finance critic on second reading debate on Bill C-57. He pointed out that because the tax is imposed on wellhead production, or gross revenue, it is in fact a royalty on natural resources rather than a tax on corporate profit or income. Under the BNA Act, natural resources belong to the provinces and, therefore, only the provinces may impose a royalty on them. In the words of the Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), the PGRT was, therefore, "an illegitimate revenue grab by the federal Government in a field of provincial concern".

Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
Various members of my Party who spoke against the PGRT in 1981 said that it would have a disproportionate effect on various producers. One Member said:
It affects all producers equally, even though all producers are not equal, either in size, in origin or in terms of whether they are genuinely independent Canadian companies.
The finance critic of the day for the New Democratic Party went on to point out that the smaller producing and exploring companies tend to be Canadian while the larger, more diversified companies are usually multinationals which could more easily absorb the tax than smaller competitors who would likely be forced out of business by it. He said the PGRT will:
-have the effect of not increasing Canadianization of the industry but decreasing it. That tax and its effect will fall more heavily on smaller companies simply engaged in the production of oil and gas. These companies do not do anything else .... This will have a lesser net impact on the cash flow of the larger multinationals.
Our present energy critic, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) elaborated on this point months later. He argued that, since the goal of the National Energy Policy was to increase Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industry, the PGRT would have the opposite effect to what is intended by the National Energy Policy because, before the imposition of the PGRT, small Canadian companies reinvested the money they made when they found oil and gas and sold it. Some of the multinational oil companies liked to take a profit and send it to their American shareholders or put it into solar energy or coal or other investments in other jurisdictions. The case was made earlier today that that has taken place, presently takes place, and will likely take place in the future.
The effect of the PGRT would be to seriously jeopardize the existence of the smaller Canadian producers while only making a marginal dent in the profits of the larger, multinational companies. That point was made by our present energy critic. He said that the New Democratic Party would have preferred an income tax measure which would allow the Government to discriminate between Canadian and nonCanadian companies, as it said it intended to do in order to increase Canadianization of the national energy policy.
A number of western Canadian members of the New Democratic Party spoke out at the time against the PGRT because we felt it discriminated against western provinces. It was a tax on oil and gas, primarily resources of Alberta and Saskatchewan, but also, to a lesser degree, of British Columbia. We felt this was a discriminatory piece of legislation aimed specifically at western producers. While a special tax was being imposed on the primary products of western Canada, no similar tax was being imposed on the primary nonrenewable resources of central and eastern Canada such as nickel, lead, zinc, copper and other commodities. It is fair to say that this tax hurt co-operative federalism and discriminated very much against the western part of the country.
I suspect that my hon. friend, the Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), will be rushing out to read all the speeches made by members of the New Democratic Party in 1980 and
1981 when this Bill was originally introduced. I know of his interest in the history of this issue. At that time a number of New Democrats made the point that this tax would dampen activity in the oil and gas industry and throw people out of work. Goodness knows that in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia thousands of men and women have been thrown out of work because of the decline in the oil and gas industry. Various speakers made the point that people are losing their jobs because the national energy policy is imposing a tax which is driving rigs out of the country. In one speech which I gave I said:
Marginal wells will be closed because they are expensive to operate and this new tax being levied makes the difference. We will see wells that could successfully be providing us with energy resources for years to come being closed off because they will no longer be economically viable.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think it would be appropriate to do so as I have made my case. In conclusion, we are pleased to support this Bill, and to have assisted all along to expedite its passage. We are pleased that it will be concluded before Christmas of 1986. However, I want to make it very clear that this does very little to help the small oil and gas exploration companies in western Canada. These are the companies which we depend upon to find new resources. The legislation does a great deal for the large integrated multinationals, Shell, Texaco, Imperial Oil and so on. They are very pleased with this legislation.
I would like to conclude by reading from an editorial which sums up today's discussion very well.
It states:
No wonder Calgary oil executives clapped approvingly on Monday when federal Energy Minister Marcel Masse told them that the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax (PGRT) would be lifted effective October 1. Masse was answering the prayers of Canada's oil giants-including multinationals such as Imperial Oil, Shell and Texaco-just when depressed international prices are pinching industry pocketbooks hard.
There can be no doubt which companies will benefit most from the government's decision to accelerate by 28 months its plan to phase out the tax-at an estimated cost of $1.5 billion to the federal treasury.
They are the biggest oil companies, the firms that make up the Canadian Petroleum Association, which lobbied heavily for the tax break and whose members account for 90 per cent of Canada's oil production, 76 per cent of the industry's workers and 80 per cent of PGRT revenues.
Yet these recipients of Ottawa's largesse aren't necessarily the neediest oil companies.
Indeed, when one looks at the various quarterly reports one can see that Imperial Oil's refining and marketing arm reported a profit for the third quarter of this year of $19 million, compared with $16 million for the same period last year. As a matter of fact, Imperial Oil's refining and marketing profits totalled $95 million. In the last number of months these companies have done extremely well, particularly in the refining and marketing sector. The fact is that this primarily helps the giant companies and does little for the small Canadian companies.

I have to admit that the author of this major shift is the Deputy Prime Minister who has had such a long career in the area of transportation during his public life.
The current regulatory regime was put in place in 1967, I believe by a gentleman elected from Newfoundland in the person of Mr. J.W. Pickersgill, that well known Newfoundland representative. Since then, of course, the world economy, our economy and the transportation industry have changed significantly, but the regulatory regime in transportation in Canada has not kept pace.
What is the result of that, Mr. Speaker? Our regulatory regime today impedes-that is the tendency-rather than supports economic development. It stifles competition in all modes of transportation. It reduces the competitiveness of our producers and the free movement of goods and people. If we do not have an efficient and effective transportation system, everyone who manufactures goods or provides services here in Canada is at a disadvantage compared with their competitors in the rest of the world. That is why these bills are known as the freedom to move legislation. They are to send a message to Canadian business and the traveller. We are freeing the transportation sector from the shackles of heavy handed economic regulation.

As a Minister and Member from that province I intend to ensure that transportation plays its proper role in particular initiatives for regional development. We have to recognize that this depends on a host of factors, not simply on one. There is nothing simple about it. Those factors are influenced by the federal and provincial Governments. That is why co-operation and a sense of fair play are needed. In other words, it is not just good enough to say that transportation must give way to regional development and overcoming regional disparity must be the one and only principle. It is one factor. We have achieved a much more co-operative relationship with the provinces and we will continue to consult with them on how transportation can contribute to the success of economic development plans. However, co-operation is a twoway street and I for one do not intend always to keep turning the other cheek. I am the type that runs out of cheeks fairly quickly.
Transportation assistance programs which benefit particular regions will continue. We have the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act. They benefit Atlantic Canada to the tune of more than $75 million a year. The Western Grain Transportation Act provides something like $600 million a year to help the grain-growing region. The new Bill recognizes the unique transportation needs of northern Canada as well. It introduces beneficial aspects of competition but maintains safeguards to protect essential air services and marine resupply to northern communities.
I want to pay tribute to the work done by the Standing Committee on Transport. Its members looked at the principle of freedom to move one year ago. They travelled about the country and suggested changes, including recommendations regarding the North. I am sure they are going to have a very important influence on this legislation and will leave their mark on it. I also know it will be done in a co-operative and consultative manner and the Chairman of the standing committee will not just run off on a frolic of his own every now and then and announce major changes to the legislation without at least telling the Minister what he is going to do.

National Transportation Act, 1986

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We have before us now a made in Canada transportation policy.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It reflects this country's special needs and concerns. It is not patterned on the U.S. It is our own. We have heard from an immense number of people and we listened to them in putting the legislation together. We know that some who work in the system feel trepidation at the prospect of change. That is natural. They are worried about what might come about as a result of changes in the status quo. We are hoping to persuade them that if they look at this with an open mind the changes are well worth any risk they feel there might be.
All of us in the transportation field are going to have to make some adjustments and display imagination and flexibility. We intend to monitor the effects of change on employees. We are not going to forget them. The offer to consult with representatives of employees and employers to identify adjustment measures which might be required above and beyond those which already exist still stands.
I met the other day with Nancy Rich, Bob White and other representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress to listen to their views. We will continue to meet with them whenever they wish to. I do not anticipate that additional adjustment measures will be necessary but it may turn out they will be. The new legislation is not just to create or preserve jobs in other sectors of the economy; it is to help create and maintain jobs in transportation itself. That can only be done if the demands of travellers and shippers increase in a growing economy.
I mentioned our Crown corporations and how they have to adapt to this system as well. I want CN, Air Canada and VIA Rail to have the greatest possible freedom to manage their business affairs in a business-like manner. They are expected to be effective, efficient, and to operate as good corporate citizens. It was the previous Liberal Government which made that principle clear with reference to CN in 1978. The company was to stand on its own feet and not receive financial assistance from the Government. Therefore, they had to be permitted to operate in the most effective and efficient manner possible.
What about the specifics? In the air mode we have a special regulatory regime in the North which includes parts of five provinces and both territories. In the rest of the country economic regulation of air services will be reduced significantly. No longer will virtually every aspect of airline operation be regulated. At the moment the setting of fares, establishing of routes, schedules and types of aircraft to be used is all regulated. The CTC has eased application of many of those regulations, but further progress is impossible without legislative reform. As a matter of fact, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), as Minister of Transport, started the process of deregulation in the air.


December 19, 1986
National Transportation Act, 1986
The test of public convenience and necessity has been used to limit entry and restrict competition in the airline industry, and that will be replaced. This has frustrated entrepreneurs for years. They saw a demand for service and wanted to fill it but were not allowed to. We think the air transport market should be open to competitive-minded, enterprising companies. All they will need in the future is to demonstrate that they are fit willing and able to provide air services. The new company will have to be Canadian-controlled, carry adequate liability insurance and, most important, will have to prove it can meet the safety standards of the Aeronautics Act. If they demonstrate those things, they will be granted a licence.
We think new companies will be encouraged to enter the market and existing companies will offer new services. We believe competition will benefit air cargo shippers as well as air travellers. Airlines will be able to adapt quickly to changes in the market-place. If they see an emerging demand and feel they can fill it, they will be able to do so without the delay and expense of licensing hearings and bureaucratic red tape and appeals. They will be free to change fares in response to marketing conditions without reference to regulatory agencies. We believe that for many small communities this new freedom to move will mean better service and competitive fares. Large carriers with large aircraft and inconvenient or infrequent service will increasingly be replaced by smaller entrepreneurs who know local conditions and requirements and can provide convenient and more frequent service. Jet aircraft, inefficient on short hops or half full, will be replaced by more suitable aircraft operating efficiently at affordable prices and at more convenient times. This is occurring in many parts of the country now and greater choices are available. Many of the new regional air carriers are using Canadian-made aircraft, in particular the Dash-7 and Dash-8 made by de Havilland. That is a tremendous spin-off benefit of this policy. The activity at de Havilland is quite remarkable. In Atlantic Canada we have Air Nova and Air Atlantic, both using Dash-7s and Dash-8s.
There are two important safeguards for the public in the new air provisions. The carriers will not be permitted to charge fares and rates in excess of those published or displayed. They are forbidden to do that. On routes served by only one airline, increases in regular air passenger fares will be appealable to the new national transportation agency which can order a reduction and refund if the increase is found to be unreasonable.
Exit from the market is also simplified under Bill C-18. A carrier will be able to discontinue or reduce a service if it provides 60 days notice to the public. That period will give other carriers the opportunity to add the route or time of service. It will also enable an airline to try out a new service without becoming rigidly locked into a money-losing proposition. With reduced risk, more innovation should follow.
To ensure that existing essential air services are not lost in any part of the country, please note that the Act empowers the
Minister of Transport to authorize direct or indirect financial assistance. If it is necessary to keep existing essential air services going, the Act will permit the Minister to do this. We do not expect that to occur often.
I mentioned the additional safeguards which have been provided for the northern part of the country. Fit, willing and able will be the basic test for entry into the northern air market, but there will be an additional test for new services in the North. Any interested party which feels that a new service will jeopardize existing essential services may file an objection with the new National Transportation Agency. The objector will have to show that the proposed new service would lead to a significant negative impact on existing service. If that is demonstrated, the licence will not be issued.
The type of service to be provided in the North, the routes to be followed, and the communities and settlements to be served will continue to be regulated as well. To ensure that fares remain at reasonable levels, the National Transportation Agency will be empowered, on a complaint, to reduce any fare it finds to be unreasonable. Northern shippers, carriers and residents have all indicated they would welcome increased competition, but they want a gradual and controlled rate which this legislation is designed to provide.
Marine transport is also important to many northern communities for resupply services. The shipping season is short up there and it is very important that marine operations be reliable. Therefore, the provisions which apply to northern marine services are tailor-made with that in mind.
The ground rules for Canada's railway shippers and carriers will be significantly altered. At present, competition between the railways is limited and often nonexistent. They are now free jointly to discuss and set freight rates. All freight must be made public through the CTC. In other words, a shipper and a carrier cannot privately negotiate a contract which addresses their particular needs. They cannot make contracts in the way in which businesses ordinarily do. As a result, the railways operate below maximum efficiency and lose business to railway carriers in the U.S., where private contracts are permitted, and to trucking. Both shippers and carriers have called for the right to contract privately for rail services. This legislation provides for such contracts as part of our plan to encourage efficiency and competition in the rail sector.
With regard to branch line abandonment, the new agency and the Minister are given many more options to deal with applications. Grain dependent branch lines designated under the WGTA will remain exempt from abandonment proceedings. The options now are to order abandonment of branch lines which are losing money, or to order them retained and for Government to subsidize the losses of the railway. The most significant new option is to allow the Minister to use moneys, which otherwise would have had to be spent to subsidize the line, to help shippers and communities adjust to alternative services such as trucking.



December 19, 1986

The Bill also has three competitive access provisions: extended interswitching limits, terminal running rights, and competitive line rates. All those provisions will assist captive shippers, that is, shippers which have access to only one railway. Those shippers will now have far greater bargaining power on rates and services, and railways will, in the future, have to compete with one another for traffic from the captive shippers.

speechtext:
The captive shipper and Canada need better service at better prices to meet the ever-increasing rigours of domestic and international competition. Captive shippers want, and should have, the right to bargain. That is what this legislation will give them. That is why I believe the Official Opposition will support this Bill. These rail reforms represent a balanced package, a redressing of the balance between shippers and carriers. We think that everyone can be a winner under these new rules. We know that everyone does not agree. The Bill is naturally a compromise and we hope that everyone will see that that is the case.
Canadian railways will be better able to compete with each other and with American railways for transborder traffic. Greater efficiency will help them secure existing jobs and create new ones in all the industries which depend on rail transportation. There are important regulatory reforms with regard to trucking contained in Bill C-19.
National Transportation Act, 1986
In 1954, the Government of Canada delegated its regulatory responsibilities for extra-provincial trucking to the provinces which all developed their own regulatory regimes. In different provinces there were different requirements for entry, for routes, for rates, for commodities, for safety precautions and so on.
That situation has made the job of meeting the needs of shippers more difficult than it needed to be. However, as the trucking industry grew and matured, regulation was reduced in all provinces, particularly in recent years. Truckers now have greater freedom to compete within the industry and with the railways. However, truckers remain saddled with a regime which limits growth and innovation. It is also inconsistent from province to province. It restricts services and imposes unnecessary costs on the industry, its customers, and on our economy. This is no way to meet future needs. In trucking, the task has involved federal and provincial Governments, the industry, producers and shippers in consultation over a number of years. A broad consensus developed that we need less regulation and more uniformity in regulation of trucking across Canada.
A historic agreement on regulatory reform of the trucking industry was reached in February, 1985, under the aegis of my colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), by all the provinces, the territories and the federal Government. The new Motor Vehicle Transport Act puts that agreement into law. However, some of the provinces are starting to backslide and say "but, if' and "but, what", indicating that the agreement does not contain that to which they agreed. As the pressure mounts more may attempt to take what they consider to be the safer way out. It is important to remember that everyone agreed in February, 1985, that there had to be regulatory reform of the trucking industry. The federal Government has the courage, the initiative and the guts to carry on with it no matter what the obstacles.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Effective January 1, 1988, there will be a uniform, nation-wide licence standard for trucking based on a new fitness test. That will consist primarily of safety and insurance requirements. The shippers would like that to be the end of the story. They would like to have the full benefits of competition as soon as possible. The industry, however, and Governments involved are convinced that an abrupt end to strict regulation might cause too many problems of adjustment. Therefore, we are including a transition phase to ease the adjustment. It will be a three-year period during which licence applications will continue to be subject to a public interest test. Those who object to the licensing of new trucking operations can still object, but the onus will be on them to prove that public harm will result if a new licence is granted.
The Bill also abolishes the extra provincial tariff approvals and route restrictions. We believe this will lead to increased competition and efficiency in the trucking industry.

December 19, 1986
National Transportation Act, 1986
Shippers will have a wider choice of carriers, enabling them to get their goods to market more quickly and efficiently. This will mean greater market opportunities, expanded sales and more jobs across Canada.
I mentioned earlier that in October we reached an agreement with the provinces and the industry on a uniform national safety code for trucking. We have agreed to a joint plan of implementing the code at the same time that the new economic regulations come into force in 1988.
Let me return to Bill C-18. What about the role of the new National Transportation Agency? The Canadian Transport Commission is the current regulatory body in transportation and carries a lot of clout. Under existing legislation, it can regulate air fares and examine any rail freight rate. It stipulates where carriers can and cannot go, what kind of services they can offer and with whom they can compete. It intervenes in disputes, holds extensive hearings and controls access to new transportation markets. It is a huge albatross about the necks of those involved in the transportation industry, and has enormous authority.
With the changes I am outlining today, which put the emphasis on competition, we need an agency that better reflects the new approach of our freedom to move legislation. It will be the new National Transportation Agency.
Its functions and powers will be tailored to this more flexible approach. It will reflect its mandate to fit regulation to the needs of people, rather than fitting people to the regulation. That is something that strikes terror into the hearts of the socialists and those who believe in state authority, and that they should regulate our every breath. We heard them asking questions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). They want us to be governed by whom we can or cannot contribute to. We should only contribute to those to whom the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) or the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) want us to contribute to. They are leading us toward the society of Big Brother. That is not the society for which we are headed. We want the more flexible approach of the National Transportation Agency and we will fit the regulations to the needs of the people.

speechtext: What are you going to do with the Newfoundland railway in this competitive environment?

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT

You have asked a good question. It deserves an answer sometime.
Unlike its predecessor, the new agency will not exercise strict economic regulatory control. As the Government that represents the people, we will set transportation policy and be responsible for it. We will not slough off responsibility to someone else because we are not involved in a Liberal slough-off regime. This is a regime of responsibility.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What are you going to do about the Newfoundland railway?

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
From time to time we may provide policy direction to the Newfoundland railway, and to the NTA. We may ask it to conduct general inquiries, but for the most part it will administer the remaining regulations and help resolve individual shipper-carrier disputes.
There will be a process for appealing agency decisions. The new dispute resolution provisions in the legislation are especially important. They put the onus squarely on the parties involved to attempt to settle conflicts before going to the National Transportation Agency. Surely it is sensible to have the parties resolve their disputes before going to the agency. This is an absolute work of genius, I say to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Let me give an example of how it will work. Suppose a large coal producer and the railway serving it cannot agree on a price to move the coal from the company's mine to market. At the request of both parties, the National Transportation Agency will be empowered to appoint a mediator to seek to resolve the dispute.
Another alternative is final offer arbitration. It is a new concept in our transportation law. The shipper may ask the agency to appoint an arbitrator to choose between its final offer and the final offer submitted by the carrier. The decision of the arbitrator will be binding for at least one year, unless the two parties can come to an alernative agreement in the meantime. In other words, it is "put up or shut up". The Member from Prince Rupert has difficulty understanding the "put option" and the "call option". Of course, I do not blame him because he is the average NDP transportation expert. This means that "put options" and "call options" are somewhat difficult for them to understand. They have been putting it to the people for years but have not yet been called upon to answer for it.
This Bill also simplifies investigations into matters of public interest. Upon receiving a complaint from a shipper, carrier or other interested party, the National Transportation Agency will have the authority to inquire into any carrier's rates, acts or omissions where the public interest may be prejudiced.
We are trying to provide maximum flexibility in the legislation. We know that it may have to be fine tuned and that there may be unforeseen developments to which we will have to respond.
The National Transportation Agency will review the operation of the legislation on an annual basis. In addition, a comprehensive review of the legislation will be undertaken by the Government in four years. It provides for annual reports, and the four-year review will be tabled in Parliament.
This is a made-in-Canada policy which balances the interests of all and the benefits to all Canadians. We believe that it will lead to more jobs and stronger regional economies. They will be stronger because there is a more reliable, efficient transportation system serving businesses there.
December 19, 1986

We think the legislation will bring about and provide for road, rail, air and marine services that can deliver goods and people more quickly, in a way that they can afford without excessive regulation, and that it will bring about competitive fares. It will result in flexible transportation networks that can adapt to new demands for services and new market opportunities. It will protect those who need protection. Public interest will be safeguarded, including the highest public interest, which is safety. It is all part of this made-in-Canada package.
We recognize the need for change and the result is this legislation. We want to thank all those who helped us, including the shippers, carriers, provincial and territorial Governments, Members of the House and the Standing Committee on Transportation which has produced two reports. 1 was especially pleased to note that the members of the committee who are of the Liberal persuasion agreed with the freedom to move proposals in many respects. I presume that means they will support this Bill in principle but, of course, damn every detail in the Bill. Nevertheless, I would sooner have them inside the tent, doing this in an outward direction, rather than outside the tent doing it in an inward direction. Of course, we do not think the NDP will see the light, but they have the Christmas period in which to consider the Bill.
It is time to get on with the job of making these changes a reality. The Deputy Prime Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) place a high priority, as do I, on this legislation. I invite all Members of the House to join with us in completing the job as quickly as possible.
This does not mean that we are no longer listening. We anticipate that during committee stage, Members will examine the Bills carefully and will hear from all interested groups. There will be good, workable suggestions for improvement and we will consider them seriously.
