speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank Hon. Members for agreeing to proceed expeditiously with this measure. On one hand its purpose and objective are simple, on the other hand its results and consequences are a matter of great urgency.

I would like to begin by quoting part of a letter from a Canadian spokesman for a parish in Hull which had sponsored a young Kampuchean. It reads:
As a student, he is not in positon to repay this by himself, but it is only fair that this money goes back to the Government, especially in the view of helping more refugees to start a new life. In particular, our parish has undertaken to sponsor his parents, and this is another instance where funds will be required for a transportation loan.
As a Canadian citizen, I am very proud and supportive of what my Government does to help refugees, and I am very satisfied-
If this Bill is not passed before the end of this calendar year, we will have to curtail the refugee movement until it is passed. This will make it most difficult for Canada to meet its international commitment to accept 12,000 refugees during 1987, and the entire refugee program would be severely disrupted. At the very least, refugees will be faced with an additional one, two or three months' wait in refugee camps. Family reunification would also be delayed as spouses and children will have to wait until new funds are available before they can be given loans to assist them to come to Canada.
The transportation loan fund was first established in 1951 to aid immigrants who could not afford the passage to Canada, to aid immigrants joining their families in Canada, refugees seeking a new life and people whose occupational skills were in demand in Canada. The fund is a revolving one and is
replenished as the loans are paid back. Although the original ceiling on the loans fund was $3 million, it has been necessary over the years to increase this amount to keep pace with rising costs resulting from inflation and the number of loan applicants. The last increase to $60 million was on May 7, 1980. This means that no more than $60 million may be lent at any one time.
A $60 million fund is not adequate to provide for our ongoing immigration transportation program because a shortfall has resulted from the large amount lent to the 60,000 Vietnamese refugees admitted in the early 1980s. Put simply, a large percentage of this money remains due because a huge sum is being repaid at a very slow rate mainly due to the employment difficulties encountered by this group of refugees.
I am pleased to say that since its inception the Canadian Government has lent $177.5 million to immigrants and refugees. Of this amount, the Government has had to write off only $4.4 million or 2.48 per cent. This is over a period of 35 years. The majority of the loans are made to refugees interest free and these loan recipients are very conscious of their responsibilty to repay the loan. They fully realize that the dollars they return to the fund would be used to bring other refugees to Canada.
Since 1970, over $94 million worth of loans has been provided to refugees. To this day, only $77,000 of this amount has been written off. That is a very low percentage. Since its beginning, the fund has served Canada well. Canada has been able to respond quickly to requests from the international community to help victims of world disasters such as the British flood victims in the 1950s, the Italian earthquake victims in 1980. The request from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees to assist the Hungarians in 195657, the Czechoslovakians, the Vietnamese and, more recently, in the Polish difficulties have been responded to with assistance from the transportation loans fund.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, family reunification has always been a cornerstone of our immigration policy. There is a favourable side effect to this policy. It has been proven that a refugee or immigrant adapts at a quicker pace if the spouse and children are in Canada. The whole family adjusts to Canadian ways together and there is no cultural gap within the family unit. The loan fund has been the instrument which has enabled the refugee to have the spouse and children join him or her that much sooner.
I have already noted that we have had some response from a number of sources. I would like to end my comments today in encouraging members of the Opposition, all Hon. Members in fact, to support the quick passage of this Bill. I would like to read from two letters received by the Government with respect to the transportation loan fund. The first correspondence is from a young Vietnamese family of three living in Niagara Falls, Ontario, who sent a card which states on the cover: "Thanks so much". What really warms our hearts is the handwritten note inside which says:
December 19, 1986

To,
The Immigration of Canada,
Dear,
We are deeply thank to our immigration and the Canadian Government, was helping my family immigrate in Canada. Thank to this great favourite.
While the words may not be exact, the meaning is clear.
Finally, the following are extracts from a note from a young man from Poland who writes:
I would like to take this opportunity, send my last payment, to thank you for entering me the door to Canada and giving me the opportunity to live in this well established and peaceful country.
This year, in April, I became a Canadian citizen. A few months ago I got an interesting job. Very shortly, I will be continuing my education through part time courses in university. I got married in June 1986. It seems that I have adopted well in Canada.
Once more, thank you, Canada, for your help!
That concludes the Government's representation to Hon. Members with respect to extending this loan fund from $60 million to $90 million so that we may fulfil our obligations in the manner in which Canada has always done on behalf of refugees and immigrants who wish to enter our country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to make some very brief comments on Bill C-34. As I indicated, in keeping with the spirit of Christmas, the Official Opposition is prepared to co-operate fully with the Government to ensure the speedy passage of Bill C-34 in all stages this afternoon. I say that notwithstanding the fact that it is literally Christmas Eve and within a few hours we will adjourn for the Christmas break. Yet the Government is asking us to deal with a piece of legislation which, it says, if it is not passed by the end of the calendar year the refugee movement will be curtailed until it is passed. We must take some exception to being lectured by the Government at the eleventh hour telling us that, if we do not pass this Bill, somehow the magnanimous doors that have been flung open in the past by the Liberal Party to refugees will be shut.
We have been here for two years since the new Government took office. Why did it not bring this piece of legislation forward sooner? It is not as if there has been a material change in circumstance overnight or over the last week. The problem which this Bill addresses could have been recognized some time ago.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this is not a lengthy Bill. Bill C-34 amends the Immigration Act. It states:
Subsection 121(3) of the Immigration Act, 1976 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(3) The total amount of outstanding advances to the Minister under this section shall not at any time exceed ninety million dollars."
As the Parliamentary Secretary has indicated, the $90 million figure replaces the $60 million figure which is in the present Act. I am pleased to note that since the inception of this fund some 35 years ago only $4.4 million has had to be
Immigration Act, 1976
written off. From this fund the Government has lent $177.5 million to immigrants and refugees to facilitate their passage to Canada. These are not grants which the Government gives but loans. The Government of 1951 which was responsible for setting up this fund ought to be congratulated for what it did back then in terms of implementing a transportation fund to assist refugees to come to Canada. It is interesting that only $4.4 million, or 2.48 per cent, of this $177 million has had to be written off.
What does that tell us? It tells us that the people who received these loans have paid them back. I challenge Hon. Members to find any other government programs in which loans are granted to students, business people or farmers who have write-off rates of 2.48 per cent. I do not imagine we could find many such programs. The point is that over this period of 35 years we have learned that the recipients of these loans are God-fearing, tax-paying citizens. And they are good ones. They recognize the obligations they have as a result of borrowing money from the Government of Canada, and they have paid that money back.
As the Parliamentary Secretary pointed out, the last increase to this transportation fund was in 1980 when it was increased to $60 million. I do not wish to repeat what the Parliamentary Secretary has said. However, it is clear that the fund must be replenished. It is clear that the Minister must have the authority to increase the fund to $90 million. We in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition are prepared to offer our full co-operation in this regard.
In closing, as a member of the parliamentary wing of the Liberal Party of Canada I take great pride in what the Liberal Party has accomplished over the last three or four decades in terms of our immigration policy. I believe very strongly, as I am sure Members on all sides of the House do, that we have one of the finest immigration policies in the world. Canada has a record and a reputation in the world for assisting and welcoming people of all races, creeds and religions to our shores. Of course, we have been critical in the last two years with respect to some of the policies of the Government. However, today is not the day to be overly critical in view of the fact that Christmas is but six days away.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to speak to Bill C-34 which will raise the total loan limit for transportation for selected refugees from $60 million to $90 million. That is to say that at no time can more than $90 million be out on loan.
The fact that there has been no increase in this amount in the last six years, a time in which transportation costs have increased by 50 per cent and the number of refugees has increased, makes it quite obvious that if we are to carry on the program this increase is necessary. As has already been pointed out, there is little danger of loss of money from this revolving loan account since less than 2.5 per cent of it has not been repaid.

December 19, 1986
Immigration Act, 1976
I think there are very few Canadians who know about this loan fund or even why it exists. It is those who have benefited from it who know about it. I agree with the previous speakers who have said that there is great gratitude for what has been done. However, I wish to say something about the basis of this program. It has been said by a very great Canadian teacher, Rabbi Plaut, who himself came here as a refugee, that there is a price we Canadians must pay for living in a country that is wealthier and more secure than most countries in the world. Part of that price is our obligation to help people who are in serious political or similar troubles arising out of conflict and oppression. These are refugees and there are 10 million or 15 million of them in the world, mostly in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Most of them do not come to Canada. They do not want to and it would not be practical for them to do so. However, some of them do need to come here. Some have been selected from the many by our officers overseas. The problem lies in getting them and their families here. This program is designed to lend them the money to pay for their travel to Canada in the certain knowledge that the very great majority of them will, when they arrive, work to repay these loans.
A few months ago, I had the privilege of visiting Guatemala in Central America. I learned that our embassy there made it possible for 750 people to escape from Guatemala in 1985. They escaped because they had to escape and they convinced our embassy, case by case, that their lives were in danger. Technically they were not refugees according to the Geneva definition because they were still in their own country, but that did not make them any safer. There were death squads threatening not only political opponents of the Government but trade union officers, school teachers, priests, teachers of catechism and anyone who was independent of the military dictatorship that ruled that country so harshly.
People were not simply being killed. Sometimes the situation was worse. I spoke to a woman who, along with her husband, was engaged in asking questions about the Government. One day her husband did not come home. He has not come home since then, but no one has told her if her husband and her daughter's father is alive or dead. A body has never been identified. To this day, she does not know if she is a widow or if she is still married. It is a terrible strain.
Families like the one to which I just referred who have been threatened often find that they cannot stand it any longer and have to get out. They get out by going to our embassy and, on the basis of the facts shown and acknowledged by embassy staff, they come to Canada. One step in that process is the provision of air fare for which most of them could never come near to paying, particularly since the value of Guatemalan currency has dropped to about one-third of what it was a couple of years ago.
In 1985, 750 people were brought out of Guatemala. This loan fund provided part of the means to make that possible. I am very proud of Canada for doing this. This is the kind of
thing that justifies the decision made a few weeks ago to give Canada the Nansen Medal for the work not just of the Government, not just of certain people but of the Canadian taxpayers through a fund like this.
I am very happy to support this Bill. I do not mind at all the fact that it comes before the House at the end of the year. It had to come before the House sometime, and why should it not come before the House during the Christmas season?

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that I have unlimited time as I stand in my place on third reading debate. I wish to assure the Members of this House that, as is my right, I intend to exercise the option of not using unlimited time today. I intend to be limited in my remarks. I hear an audible sigh of relief from the benches across the way, and an audible sigh of disappointment from both the NDP and Liberal camps.
I wish to take this opportunity as this Bill flies through the House. This Bill affects the way in which the salary scales are determined for the Lieutenant Governors of the 10 provinces of Canada. This Bill affects those ordinary citizens who have been elevated to a position of ceremonial responsibility; in fact, constitutional authority when necessary-ceremonial largely and constitutional occasionally. We saw that in Ontario very recently where the Lieutenant Governor made a very wise and proper decision.
I wish to take this opportunity to indicate that at some point it would be wise for the House and the Government to produce a paper advising the people of Canada, and inviting Members of Parliament to participate in the discussion on the criteria used in choosing Lieutenant Governors. In that manner, Lieutenant Governors may arise from the relative obscurity that sometimes enshrouds the office and take their proper place within the Canadian establishment and system. That can best be utilized when Canadians have a better understanding of how it is that Governments, the Government of Canada and provincial Governments, come to a decision as to who the Lieutenant Governor of a province should be.
I believe that the Lieutenant-Governor who was recently named for the Province of Newfoundland, the former Member for St. John's East, was a long-time servant of this Parliament and an extraordinary parliamentarian. Joey Smallwood in Newfoundland holds the title of the last living Father of Confederation. It can truly be said that Jim McGrath, who is no longer a Member and I can use his name-outside this Chamber, of course, it is His Excellency-is the father of reform in this Parliament. He would endorse my suggestion today that the process by which we select Lieutenant Governors ought to be opened up and examined more closely, so that these positions are more relevant to the public at large.
Let me take this opportunity to wish all Lieutenant Governors, but in particular the Lieutenant-Governor of Newfoundland, a very Merry Christmas, all the best in the New Year, and to tell them that after only such a short period of time, a few weeks or months since he has been Lieutenant Governor, we in Newfoundland see in him a gentleman who has brought a fresh surge of energy, life, and relevance to the post. We are proud. Mr. Speaker, you know that I am a man who always speaks in a non-partisan way, so this comment will not be unusual coming from me. We are indeed proud to this date of the manner in which he has upheld his office.

Mr. Speaker, as a Member from the Province of Ontario, I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about our Lieutenant Governor. As you know, the Hon. Lincoln Alexander is a former Member of the House of Commons. He was not from this side of the House but a Conservative Member of Parliament from the opposite side. I am very proud and honoured to have the Hon. Lincoln Alexander as our Lieutenant Governor. I had the opportunity to meet with him for the first time at a dinner in my riding some months ago. I greatly admire the work he is doing as the Liuetenant Governor of the province. He is a true gentleman and a great Canadian.
And a super Tory.

My colleague, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) rhetorically asked how Lieutenant Governors are chosen and what process is taken. The Hon. Lincoln Alexander shared his experience with us. He read in a newspaper that he was being considered for the position of Lieutenant Governor. He was deeply honoured to know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was considering appointing him. He waited for the phone call. He told us that his legs were shaking when the voice at the other end of the line asked whether he would like to be the next Lieutenant Governor of the Province of Ontario.
In closing, allow me as a Member from Ontario to express my personal season's greetings, on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada and I am sure on behalf of all Members of the House of Commons and to express our sincerest best wishes to Lieutentant Governor, the Hon. Lincoln Alexander, and his family.

Hear, hear!

There are two report stage motions on today's Notice Paper in the name of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), in amendment to Bill C-7. I regret, but I must rule that Motion No. 1 is out of order in that it seeks to amend the interpretation clause of the Bill. I refer the Hon. Member to Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 773 (10) which reads:
A substantive amendment may not be introduced by way of a modification to the interpretation clause of a bill.
December 19, 1986

Motion No. 2 is in order and shall be put to the House.

Motion No. 2
That Clause 2 be amended by striking out lines 20 to 26 at page 1 and
substituting the following therefor:
"ministerial record" means a record created or received by a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of a Minister, in the course of conducting actitities which relate to the carrying out of the statutory duties of the Minister;
She said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to my amendment which would change the clause on the definition of ministerial record which presently reads:
"Ministerial record" means a record of a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of a Minister and that pertains to that office, other than a record that is of a personal or political nature or that is under the control of a Government institution.
My argument is based on the fact that the present definition defines a ministerial record by what it is not, not by what it is. It is not political, it is not personal, according to this definition, nor under the care and control of a government institution. I would suggest that that is not a very constructive way to determine what is a ministerial record. I would like to recommend my proposed amendment because I believe my definition brings into much clearer focus the kind of information and documentation we would like to hold in the Archives of Canada which would be an ongoing record for all time as to the role, accomplishment and function of the particular Minister in question.
The proposed amendment came out of a fair amount of research on our part. This was directed by the prior Minister of Communications who had suggested we look most carefully to definitions and descriptions throughout the democratic world as we know it and to those public archival institutions that exist elsewhere. As a result, the proposed amendment flows most particularly from the American definition of presidential record. The other models we looked at were the British, the American and the Australian, but this one seemed the most constructive one that I could find, and I submit that the definition of ministerial record will be much clearer. We heard considerable testimony about the lack of clarity and the breadth of documents that could escape the archival control from the Association of Manitoba Archivists, from the Manitoba Council of Archives, from L'Institut D'Histoire de I'Amerique Frangaise who argued that a clearer definition of what constitutes a ministerial record be found. In their view, it should be made clear that all ministerial records stemming from Government activity or involving a Minister in the conduct of official business, including documents relating to the formulation of policy or to be deemed public records and transferred to the archives when the use for which they were orginally created ceased. The present definition is more in the nature of what it is not rather than what it is.
In light of the fact that my other amendment has been ruled out of order as beyond the interpretation of the Bill, I respectfully suggest that this amendment would allow things like
Archives of Canada Act
royal commission studies that would fall under the Inquiries Act to be commissioned by a Minister. It would then be part and parcel of the record in our archives. It is quite surprising that the records of CN, Air Canada and CBC will not be held, as they would fall under ministerial responsibility. Therefore, they would fall under the collective memory that we would find in our archives.
I know there was much discussion in committee with the Minister present as to the definition that I have proposed. There was concern that it might be limited. I am suggesting that the original presentation of that clause is a limited one and this would be a much broader interpretation. Therefore, I strongly suggest that the Minister accept this new definition which is brought with the best of intent to make the archives Bill function in the way in which the standing committee wished to see it function. I know it was in the interests of everyone. We were pleased to see this new revision of the Public Archives Act.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few observations in response to the proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) concerning the definition of ministerial record. The definition agreed to by the legislative committee on December 10 reads as follows:
"Ministerial record" means a record of a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of the Minister and that pertains to that office, other than a record that is of a personal or political nature or that is under the control of a government institution.
That definition sets out the three categories of records which can be found in the office of a Minister. The first is those records directly controlled by a Minister which pertain to his or her position as a Minister and member of the Queen's Privy Council of Canada. The second is those records under the control of a government institution which deal with the business of the institution. The third is the personal or political records of the Minister relating to his or her functions as a member of a political Party, representative of a federal constituency, or as a parliamentarian, or to his or her private life and interests. I believe that this is a very comprehensive definition and will serve Canadians well. The amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal is as follows:
"Ministerial record" means a record created or received by a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of a Minister, in the course of conducting activities which relate to the carrying out of the statutory duties of the Minister;"
I believe there is a serious flaw in that proposal. In referring as it does to the statutory duties of the Minister it does not cover the large class of records which relate to ministerial responsibilities and duties not based on statute. For example, the Queen's Privy Council is not a statutory body. The duties of the Minister as a member of the Cabinet are not statutory. Accordingly, the definition proposed by the Hon. Member for

December 19, 1986
Archives of Canada Act
Mount Royal would not apply to records relating to a Minister's duties as a member of Cabinet. I believe that would be a most unfortunate consequence of passing this amendment.
In short, I am fully satisfied with the current definition of ministerial record and it is my hope that this amendment will not be sustained.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). In doing so I want to indicate to the Minister that the argument she has made in, I believe improperly but not deliberately, interpreting this amendment sounds rather strange when the wording the Minister proposes says:
"ministerial record" means a record of a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of a Minister and that pertains to that office-
The argument she makes, wrongly, I believe, that this amendment would be limited in its effect is in fact the problem with her own interpretation of ministerial record. It is too limited. Her definition goes on, and this is the escape clause:
-other than a record that is of a personal or political nature or that is under the control of a government institution;
That is a huge escape clause with respect to what should be counted as ministerial record.
I think the Hon. Member for Mount Royal has done a great service to Parliament in taking the time to examine this matter closely. She has put forward an amendment based on the American model of ministerial records of responsibility. I would go so far as to say that if the definition she now has in the Bill were in place in the U.S. during the days of the Nixon presidency then the tapes of the conversation between the President of the U.S. and his aides concerning the cover-up of a break-in would never have been part of the official record.
Members opposite can chuckle, but the President would have said, according to the Minister's definition, that the break-in at the Democratic Party headquarters was a political matter. Therefore, the record of his conversations with Mr. Haldeman, Mr. Erlichman and Mr. Dean would never have been made available as they were ordered to be by the U.S. Supreme Court. They would not have been considered part of the record of the President's day-to-day activities. They would have been considered to be of a political or personal nature. Therefore, given the kind of interpretation contained in Bill C-7, Watergate could never have happened, not because the system is incapable of that kind of political activity but because the truth would never have been known. Neither the people of Canada, the nation's press or an independent judicial commission of inquiry, the Canadian equivalent of a U.S. special prosecutor, would have been able to get to the bottom of the matter because they would never have been able to obtain the records in the first place.
What we are saying to the Minister, who obviously has no fear about that kind of exposure, and her colleagues, who also obviously have no fear of that hypothetical situation in this country, is that the definition provided by the Minister allows
for an escape hatch big enough for an 18-wheel Mack truck to drive through. That is the difficulty with this definition.
The Minister should know that this amendment is proposed with the knowledge of the kind of activities which went on during Watergate and which are going on today in what is called Irangate in the U.S. A special congressional committee and a special Senate committee in the U.S. are examining all matters relating to an activity which breaches American law. In the course of their investigation they are asking for records and transcripts of phone calls and other conversations. Let me ask the Minister this: If the President of the U.S. and his chief aides and cabinet secretaries were to say "Yes, but those conversations were of a political nature, we were trying to figure out how to avoid a political fall-out", then what is the definition of a cover-up? Is it an official responsibility? It is not part of his official responsibility to cover things up. That is political. It might be illegal. Based on such criteria, we would never have a Watergate in this country because we would never get to the bottom of the barrel and find out the truth. That is why the amendment moved by the Member for Mount Royal, who has done excellent work on behalf of Canada, ought to be accepted today.

She said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to address the House as Bill C-7, an Act respecting the National Archives of Canada and to amend other Acts in relation thereto, receives third reading. On this occasion I am reminded of a similar event in our nation's history. Almost 75 years ago, in January, 1912, the Conservative Government of Robert Laird Borden introduced the first archives legislation. At that time, the archives branch had already been operating for 40 years. It had been operating for those 40 years, acquiring and conserving both public and private historical records, without benefit of a legislative mandate. That legislation came before the House in 1912.
At that time Prime Minister Borden acknowledged the essential role of the Archives when he expressed the intention of his Government to take concerted and deliberate action to ensure the preservation and safeguarding of our nation's archival heritage.
The object of the Public Archives Act was that records "no longer required for the every-day purposes of public administration-should be removed to a place of security-and classified so as to be easily accessible to those who may desire to consult them".
[ Translation]
Prime Minister Borden's proposal was supported by the Leader of the Opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the Bill was quickly adopted. In 1912, the general consensus was that the legislation met a need and was an adequate response to the general desire to preserve the historic documents of the nation.
It therefore seems appropriate for this Government to introduce a new National Archives of Canada Act to replace the outdated Act of 1912, and it is with great pride that I take this opportunity to speak to Bill C-7 today.

I would like to review, for a moment, the progress of this Bill. It first came before the House during the first session of this Parliament as Bill C-95 on February 12, 1986. It received second reading on June 11 and was referred to committee for study. The committee's examination of the legislation was well under way when the first session of this Parliament was prorogued. On October 3, 1986, all Parties agreed to reinstate the Bill at committee stage. Bill C-7 was referred to the legislative committee chaired by my colleague, the Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), who guided the committee adeptly through a number of hearings.
The co-operation which characterized the enactment of the 1912 Act has also been evident through the proceedings of this committee. The committee undertook its study with a view to making the Bill a better piece of legislation. It has succeeded. It listened to many Canadians representing archival associations, provincial organizations, learned societies, universities, historians and writers. Some submitted briefs and several
Archives of Canada Act
appeared as witnesses. The views of these individuals and groups have been invaluable. So, too, have been the contributions of the committee members. It was apparent to me when I appeared before the committee that its members share a sincere interest in our nation's archival heritage and the legislation designed to preserve it.
I am particularly pleased to advise the House that at clause by clause study of this Bill on December 10 agreement was reached on seven substantive amendments. In brief, Mr. Speaker, with regard to Clause 3(1), it was unanimously agreed to change the name of the institution to the National Archives of Canada/Archives Nationales du Canada. Similarly, it was agreed that the title of the deputy head should be National Archivist of Canada/Archiviste National du Canada. Witnesses had requested these changes to ensure that the name and title reflect Canada's federal structure, and to follow international practice.
A second substantive change, also unanimously agreed to, was the deletion of the opening words of Clause 5(1) "Except as otherwise provided under an Act of Parliament". Witnesses had unanimously requested this change. The intent of Clause 5 is, as a result, much clearer. It establishes, for the first time in law, the requirement for government institutions to obtain the consent of the archivist before destroying or disposing of their records.
As a result of a consensus reached with Departments and agencies responsible for security and intelligence matters, I was able to respond to the serious concerns of witnesses about Clauses 5(6) and 6(4). I am very pleased to report that the legislative committee unanimously approved the deletion of these sections, together with Clause 6(l)(b). I am confident that existing records management practices are fully adequate to ensure that the legitimate interests of our allies in the areas of security and intelligence are respected.
Another substantive issue on which there was agreement to amend this Bill relates to the legal deposit provisions of Clause 8(3). This passage provides for the Archives to pay the actual costs of making a copy requested under this provision of the Act. The amendment excludes government institutions and their agents from the effect of this reimbursement provision. Recordings are regularly acquired from government institutions, and it was never the intention of Clause 8 that this reimbursement provision should apply within the Government.
The final major issue on which agreement was reached in committee was the establishment and the composition of an advisory board.
Clause 9(1) had provided that the Minister might establish a board with certain ex officio members, and not more than seven members appointed by the Minister from among persons who had expertise in archival matters or who are residents of Canada.

December 19, 1986
Archives of Canada Act
The committee agreed that the Minister shall establish such a board. It also agreed that the seven other members shall be appointed by the Minister from among persons experienced in archival matters. I am convinced that this change will result in a stronger board, which will provide useful advice to the archivist.
In conclusion, I believe that we have responded to the concerns of witnesses. Their testimony was most helpful in the formulation of amendments. I also wish to cite the extremely co-operative role of the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) and the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). Their assistance made possible significant improvements to this Bill.
It is a pleasure for me, as a Minister of the Crown, to sponsor a Bill that has received such broad support from the Members of the House. I believe this is because we all recognize that the new national Archives of Canada Act is vital to the Canadian archival community. It is now my privilege to recommend this Bill to the House for third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) that she will have her Bill for Christmas.
I rise today to speak at third reading of Bill C-7, an Act respecting the National Archives of Canada and records of government institutions of Canada, and to amend the Copyright Act.
(Translation]
The National Archives of Canada Act will replace the present Public Archives Act which goes back to 1912. Since 1912, the Public Archives of Canada have freely interpreted the unique definition, never changed since that time, of its mandate or mission to collect and preserve historical documents of every kind, nature and description-, to justify its present day activities. These activities will now be more acurately defined in a completely revised version of the Public Archives Act, reflecting not only the scope of the Archives' present collections and the methods used to preserve them, but also the other duties and activities of the Public Archives today.
The Public Archives is an institution that is essential to the preservation of our heritage and shares this purpose with the National Museums of Canada. The importance of the institution was admirably expressed in the presentation by the Public Archives to the Applebaum-Hebert Committee, and I quote:
If the archives of a nation, a government or an organization are not preserved, then the history of that nation, government or organization will be forgotten, and the price which a people pay for the loss of their history is a misunderstanding of their roots, confusion in their identity and the misinterpretation or misrepresentation of the nature of their country.

"Of all our national treasures, the archives are the most precious. They are the legacy of one generation to another, and
the quality of care we give them testifies to the quality of our civilization". This was said more than 50 years ago by a former Dominion Archivist, Arthur G. Daughty.
During second reading of this Bill, the previous Minister of Communications gave an eloquent explanation of the importance of the Archives. I want to quote him.

If a people is not aware of its past, it has no identity. It suffers from amnesia. It does not know its strengths, it does not know its weaknesses and cannot build on its experience. It cannot leap forward because it lacks the starting block of history. It cannot legitimize its institutions or identify their responsibilities, anymore than it can determine the rights of individuals and groups.
The original identity of our country, which we defend and strengthen, each in our own way, is partly reflected in our institutions and our present day way of life, but also in the roots of the present which we can find through the archives.
These, according to Doughty, are the soul of a people, its collective memory. They are essential to a people's understanding of itself, its past, its present activity and its aspirations for the future.

I would like to add another dimension. Within the mission of the National Archives I want to underline how important it is to reflect the multicultural, multilingual background which is the tapestry and design that forms the background of Canada's beautiful landscape and guards and preserves for our children and our children's children the historical records of our society. It is from these very societies that we must seek to collect and preserve this historical documentation so that people see themselves reflected through their roots in our own archives. They are the archives of all the peoples of Canada, regardless of when they arrived on these shores.
That is one reason why I regret most sincerely that my first amendment was not accepted by the Government. It enlarged the interpretation of the Bill, because when we lose the history of the CNR or Air Canada, we lose a precious part of our heritage. There is a potential for loss when such preservation is not mandated.
Consultations with informed, interested and public minded citizens and other groups was absolutely key to this Bill's ability to truly fulfil its mandate. The considered opinions enabled the legislators in the House to perform our duties much more effectively. A key example of the vigilance that can be found in community based groups and by professional associations can be seen with respect to Clause 5(6) and Clause 6(4) of the original Bill.
In the original text of Bill C-7, before it was amended, documents relating to international relations or defence were to be exempted from the requirement that no documents be destroyed without the consent of the archivist. There were strong representations from such groups as the Social Science Federation, the Canadian Historical Association, and the Canadian Association of University Teachers, who felt that the reference to any record containing privileged information from a foreign state was far too broad. By exempting all such records from the National Archivist's control, irrespective of how much privileged information might be contained in them,
December 19, 1986

it was argued that too many valuable Canadian records could be destroyed on this ground and, therefore, lost forever. As a result of the strong arguments brought forth by these witnesses, this exemption was deleted.
In Clause 6(1 )(b) and Clause 6(4) there were similar significant exemptions. Under its terms, records containing confidential information from a foreign Government or an international organization of states, dealing with either the conduct of international affairs, the defence of Canada or any of its allies, or the prevention or suppresion of subversive or hostile activities, were exempted from the provisions under Clauses 6(1 )(b) and 6(4) unless the foreign entity in question consented to the transfer of the confidential records to the Archives. Witnesses as well were concerned about the National Archivist's ability to exercise full control over records containing valuable information. Once more, witnesses played a significant role in deletion of this clause and helped immeasurably in the improvement of this Bill.
Another significant change to the legislation was in the nomenclature. This change was proposed by the Government and myself. The former Dominion Archivist, Doctor Wilfrid Smith, the Social Science Federation of Canada, and the Association of Canadian Archivists recommended that the name given to the Archives should correspond to the existing patterns of other national cultural institutions such as the National Library, the National Arts Centre, the National Museums Corporation, and the National Film Board. We were also told during the hearings on Bill C-7 that of approximately 140 countries that are members of the International Council on Archives, approximately 130 have "National Archives" as their title. We are pleased that the Minister gave this new title to the Bill. It is now formally known as the National Archives and gives it a distinct definition from provincial archives and other municipal archives.
While I generally support Bill C-7 and am pleased with the changes passed by our legislative committee, there were two changes I would have liked to see incorporated into the new legislation. They involve the definitions given to "government institutions" and "ministerial records". The term "government institutions" is defined at Clause 2 to mean:
A government institution listed in Schedule 1 to the Access to Information Act or the schedule to the Privacy Act or any institution designated by the regulations of the Governor in Council as a government institution for the purposes of this Act.
I did not find that large enough. I regret most sincerely it was ruled out of order because I really believe that boards, commissions or Crown corporations established by or under an Act of Parliament should be included along with, as I said, Air Canada, CN and CBC.
The term "ministerial record" in turn refers to:
A record of a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who holds the office of a Minister and that pertains to that office, other than a record that is of a personal or political nature or that is under the control of a government institution.
Archives of Canada Act
That particular definition is of great ongoing concern to me and I shall come back to that as I point out what my hon. colleague just recently underscored for us.
Of those who made written submissions or appeared before the committee, the majority felt that these definitions were too narrow and vague. They argued, and I argued, strongly that the Act should also apply to the records of Parliament, royal commissions of inquiry and Crown corporations as well as other institutions not listed in the relevant schedules of the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, that is, Air Canada, the Canadian National Railway and the CBC. It was suggested as well by the Association of Canadian Archivists that judicial records also be included.
It was widely held that unless the National Archives had jurisdiction over these records, an important part of Canada's heritage might be lost. Without effective control, historically valuable records might be dispersed or destroyed and research would accordingly be extremely difficult or impossible to carry out.
The Social Science Federation of Canada expressed its understanding of the desire of vital institutions such as the CBC or Parliament to preserve their independence. However, it felt that such freedom could and should be limited slightly to ensure that historical records were fully preserved. In its view, alternative arrangements could be made. For example, records scheduled for retention to the physical custody of the originating agency, should the latter not want them to be placed in the National Archives indefinitely, would be fine. It was for these reasons that I and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), proposed amendments which would have addressed these very concerns and ensured access to records which now could potentially be lost forever.
Apart from the question of the too narrow definition of "government institution", some concern was also expressed in relation to the definition of "ministerial record". The Institut d'Histoire de I'Amerique Franqaise pointed out the difficulty of establishing a clear distinction between records of a personal or political nature on the one hand and those which strictly relate to the office of a Minister, on the other hand. It was felt that the archivists should have the right to view all ministerial records and decide, in co-operation with the Minister, what records should be preserved. Again, this clause is not truly inclusive of all the areas which should be part of our collective memory over time.
I could not have said more eloquently than my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), who expressed his concern that Watergate could not be found out now as we pass this Bill into law. He points out that this is called the "cover-up" clause. The Minister may laugh all she wishes. I hope she is correct and that I am proven incorrect. As the clause now stands, it becomes a serious cover-up clause and even the findings of the Parker Inquiry would have been damaged had this present ministerial record held and the information we required from the Archives not been

December 19, 1986
Archives of Canada Act
recovered. I hope the Minister will pay attention to that particular reservation because it is most serious.
The Association of Manitoba Archivists and the Manitoba Council of Archives argued that a clearer definition of what constitutes a "ministerial record" should be found. I believe, and the amendment I proposed tries to make clear, that all ministerial records stemming from government activities ought to be deemed "public records" and transferred to the National Archives when the use for which they were originally created ceased. Documents relating to a Minister's private life and interests, of course, and perhaps political Party and constituency files, should be considered his or her private or personal papers and could be given to the Archives as, if and when the Minister might so desire. I really quite regret the decision taken in this area.
An enormous amount of space is required to store more than the billions of items, including 11 million photographs, maps and plans and 365 million pages of federal government documents which the Archives own. At present the Public Archives' holdings are scattered among seven different buildings throughout the National Capital region in addition to the main building which it shares with the National Library on Wellington Street. Not only are the spaces insufficient but the conditions within them, which I am sure the Minister knows, pose serious threats for the long-term preservation of the collections of the historical record, information and knowledge about our cultural heritage.
They are the background documents which define us as a distinct and proud nation. They are the record upon which we can build through film and videos our own heroes. They are key to much that is our future. Those stacks are overflowing in buidings which are not protected against humidity, theft, vandalism or water damage. As each day goes by, a lot of data, part of which is significant to our history, is being erased and is disappearing. It is not because the archivists do not care, it is because they do not have the resources to do their jobs properly.
Added to this is the fact that storage space is being shared with other organizations which all supposes control and security problems. Because holdings are spread among several locations, the records frequently have to be moved about. This repeated handling is another cause of damage, as are the changes in atmospheric conditions and contamination by insects. I sincerely hope that we can do something about this because the consequences of such a situation are disastrous.
During the last four years there have been no less than 45 emergencies. In some cases there were major floods causing irreparable damage and loss. In other cases, it was simply a leak or recurring leaks which damaged the collections. Over the long term, the documents in the Archives are attacked by mildew, oxidation, dust and unnecessary wear and tear. Now that the Government will have this new legislation, I sincerely hope a new facility will soon be announced to address these problems as I believe that successive Governments have, in the
past many years, allowed this situation to arrive at such a critical state.
I would like at this moment to congratulate the Minister for bringing in this Bill. It is a fine New Year's present for Canadians as we become more sensitive to our place in world history and more appreciative of our profound cultural beauty and heritage. I hope we will have a new building to go along with the Minister's new Bill in the very new future.

Mr. Speaker, I have to concede, first, that my acquaintanceship with Archives policy has not been nearly as close as those who have sat through the excellent committee hearings that took place on this Bill. On the contrary, my role has been to use the Archives at different points in time. That is where I gleaned my knowledge of the Liberal Party in terms of its disastrous past and, hopefully, its limited future.
When the Bill was first introduced in the House it was a Bill which had in it a number of points that were quite seriously mistaken. This shows us how the parliamentary system by permitting input from sources outside the bureaucracy and outside the profession of archivists themselves is able to improve significantly on legislation.
When the Bill was first brought forward I recall making a speech in which I outlined some of the very considerable reservations which existed on the part of the Social Sciences Federation, for instance, with respect to the original Bill. It is a source of great pleasure to have seen this Bill referred to committee where the suggestions for change put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) were heard. It has been wonderful to see those changes and to see that the Bill before us is in a much improved form.
In view of this tremendous progress we recognize that this is an important piece of legislation. If my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood were here she would point out that there are areas in which problems remain, as with any piece of legislation. Therefore, I am pleased to be able to support this Bill on behalf of our Party for third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I have but a short comment to make. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) said that we needed her amendment. She said that the most glaring example which showed when we needed it was Watergate. I wish to point out to her that Watergate did not use the archives to expose the crime. It would have been a little late at that time to expose that particular incident.

I would like to take this opportunity, while we still have a few minutes left, to offer the entire staff of the House of Commons and all those people who work so hard for us, our best wishes for a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. I admit there is a new ambience in the House, and I must say it does make it more pleasant to work with the Government, although that is not necessarily always the case. However, I would also like to wish my hon. friends opposite a Merry Christmas and a Happy and Prosperous New Year, and I hope that 1987 will be a good year for us and perhaps for them as well, if they behave. [English]

However, since the opportunity has now presented itself, may I also, on behalf of our Party, express to you, Mr. Speaker, and to your colleagues, who occupy the chair at various times, our best wishes for a Merry Christmas, Happy New Year and happy holiday season. I want to thank you very much, from our standpoint, for your tremendous co-operation and support over the course of the last number of months. I also want to thank the Clerk of the House and the Table Officers for their support, as well as the Pages for the very good work they do, but most of all I appreciate the tremendous support and cooperation we received from the Table.
I wish all my hon. friends and colleagues a very happy holiday season. I know we are all extending the holiday break but I think it is well deserved. I wish you all a very happy holiday season.
